Prevention: Completely remove and bury or burn crop residues
Space or prune trees to ensure that canopies do not touch.
Destroy (burn) the pruned leaves and braches
Avoid the movement of planting material from infested areas to other areas
Destroy any existing ant colonies (ants can deter natural enemies of the mealybug)
Limit the movement of vehicles/machines through infested areas as this may spread the pest
Hibiscus, etc. in and nearby crop
Encourage the build up of natural enemies like ladybirds (e.g.
Cryptolaemus montrouzieri ), lacewings, and hover flies by reducing pesticide sprays
Monitoring: Additional relevant crops: hibiscus, avocado, citrus, cotton, tomato, eggplant, peppers, beans and peas, sweet potato, mango, cherry, and pomegranate
Weekly monitoring and scouting to detect early presence of the papaya mealybugs.
Look for: 0.3-4 mm long, yellowish, slightly flattened insects, oval-shaped with a white waxy coating.
Males are 1 mm long, tend to be pink, have long antennae and wings covered with white wax powder.
Clusters of cotton-like masses on leaves, stems or fruit
Deformation of new growth, leaf yellowing, leaf curl, distorted/small fruit, early fall of fruit
Fruit may be completely covered by a layer of mealybugs and wax secretions
Flowers may be distorted and fail to open
Ants which are harvesting honeydew from the mealybugs
Sooty mould formation due to honeydew excretions by mealybugs
Direct Control: Cryptolaemus montrouzieri ), lacewings, and hover flies feed on the mealybugs
Use sticky bands on the trunk or branches to control ants and enhance the effectiveness of natural enemies
Chemical control is difficult since the waxy covering on the body of the mealybug protects it
